definition: Edison's 1877 machine that recorded by pressing a stylus track into tinfoil on a cylinder, later wax; the first device to record and play back sound.
A device about 20 years older than the phonograph that traced sound waves but could not play them back; Edison reversed its process.
The improved cylinder machine by Bell, Bell and Tainter that replaced tinfoil with wax, patented May 4, 1886.
Emile Berliner's flat-disc system, patented November 8, 1887; the ancestor of every record since.
The first commercial record shape, a tube; Edison conceded to the disc in 1913 and made his last cylinders in 1929.
The compound used for 78s: shellac resin with fillers such as clay, slate or limestone, carbon black and cotton fibers. Heavy and brittle.
The shellac-era disc, produced commercially from 1897 to the late 1950s; speeds were not standardized, despite the name.
The wide groove used on most records made before 1948.
The narrow groove introduced with the 1948 LP; microgroove discs carry nearly twice as many grooves as coarse-groove discs.
The vinyl compound Columbia used for its first LPs, sold as nonbreakable.
The long-playing 12-inch record at 33 1/3 rpm, unveiled by Columbia in June 1948.
RCA Victor's 7-inch single at 45 rpm with a large center hole, introduced January 10, 1949.
The 1949-50 contest between Columbia's 33 1/3 and RCA Victor's 45; it ended with the LP as the album and the 45 as the single.
The deliberate bass cut and treble boost applied when cutting a record, reversed by the phono preamp on playback.
The US standard playback equalization approved January 29, 1954, still the curve phono preamps follow.
RCA Victor's equalization curve from about 1952, essentially identical to the RIAA curve.
The Westrex system that cuts left and right channels on the two walls of one groove, each at 45 degrees; the US standard from December 27, 1957.
Recording Industry Association of America; sets US record standards and publishes official US shipment and revenue figures.
British Phonographic Industry; publishes official UK sales from Official Charts Company data.
US sales tracker, formerly Nielsen SoundScan; counts consumer purchases rather than RIAA-style shipments.
An annual day of exclusive releases at independent record shops, conceived in 2007 and first held in April 2008.
